In the U.S., the firm expects operating profits to rise 27% this year, up sharply from its initial 13% forecast at the start of 2026. JPMorgan said the strength extends well beyond the biggest AI beneficiaries, with companies outside AI and energy expected to deliver roughly 10% annual profit growth this year and next. JPMorgan Asset Management sees an unusually strong global profit cycle taking shape, with corporate earnings expected to grow nearly 30% in 2026 and another 20% in 2027. The firm says the artificial intelligence investment boom remains the biggest driver of that growth, with spending on AI infrastructure expected to remain robust for years. In the U.S., the firm expects operating profits to rise 27% this year, up sharply from its initial 13% forecast at the start of 2026. JPMorgan said the strength extends well beyond the biggest AI beneficiaries, with companies outside AI and energy expected to deliver roughly 10% annual profit growth this year and next. "We have rarely seen such a strong profit cycle," JPMorgan said. Energy has also emerged as a major source of earnings growth, with sector profits rising more than 80% this year. Meanwhile, nearly 90% of S&P 500 companies are growing their earnings, JPMorgan said, which is a level near the top of the historical range. That broader earnings growth gives investors more opportunities to diversify beyond the crowded AI trade, particularly after years of extreme concentration in technology stocks. JPMorgan remains constructive on AI and expects robust spending to continue well into 2028. But the firm warned that the market has already largely priced in another strong year of AI investment in 2027, while the cost of funding that spending is becoming harder to ignore. "First, the market has already largely discounted another strong year of investment spending in 2027," JPMorgan said. "Second, we're beginning to see the strains of funding all this AI growth." Hyperscalers are increasingly turning to debt markets as AI infrastructure spending outpaces cash flow, JPMorgan said. At the same time, higher interest rates are making that borrowing more expensive. The firm noted that bonds and equities of some of the most aggressive AI spenders, including neocloud companies, have recently come under pressure. JPMorgan isn't abandoning the AI trade. Instead, it says investors should become more selective. "We remain constructive on the AI theme but with a strong preference for higher quality names," the firm said, adding that it is "carefully managing overall AI exposures and individual stock risks." That caution could also create an opening for stocks that have been left behind by the AI rally. JPMorgan said the historic collapse in momentum during July could favor previous laggards, particularly software companies that were treated as "AI losers." "The biggest lesson is that the laggards from the momentum phase tend to perform very well," JPMorgan said. title: J.P. Morgan Just Made a Bold Prediction About Bitcoin. Should You Buy It? - The Motley Fool
content: J.P. Morgan sees the coin as a better performer than stocks, though it comes at a cost. In its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report published in October 2026, J.P. Morgan projects that Bitcoin (BTC +0.96%) will return 10% annually over the next 10 years, versus its 7.5% forecast for large U.S. stocks. That call can be viewed as being very pessimistic about Bitcoin, as it's far lower than its compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 43.9% over the last four years, or as bullish, as it implies that it'll outperform every major asset class the bank models over a fairly long period of time. Given that framing, should you buy the coin and hold it through the bank's forecast period? J.P. Morgan expects 55% annual volatility for Bitcoin, and only 18% for large U.S. stocks. Both figures are broadly in line with the historical data. Using J.P. Morgan's figures for the coin's estimated forward returns versus stocks, the two earn the same 0.32 points of return above holding cash per point of volatility. That implies it does not really believe there will be a higher volatility-adjusted return with Bitcoin than with stocks, only that Bitcoin's higher expected return comes with proportionally more risk. The subtext here is that if you can't handle seeing the value of your investment swinging around a lot, Bitcoin is not going to be pleasant for you to hold even if it ultimately returns more. The factor at the heart of the projection is Bitcoin's shrinking rate of new supply being mined over time, versus the generally expanding global money supply. J.P. Morgan called the coin "a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing," meaning it's a risky asset that tends to do well when central banks expand the money supply. That mostly fits; while the coin hasn't proven it's an effective hedge against inflation, its strictly limited supply and the impossibility of printing more of it by fiat should mean its purchasing power continues to hold up over time. Per J.P. Morgan, this is the first time this report series has included a Bitcoin return forecast. It still doesn't recommend an allocation. Still, it expects Bitcoin to beat stocks over the next decade. So it's worth owning at least a little, once your traditional portfolio is sufficiently diversified. As for how much to buy, BlackRock found in December 2024 that a 2% Bitcoin allocation in a traditional 60/40 stock-and-bond portfolio accounted for 5% of its total risk, while a 4% allocation accounted for 14%. Morgan Stanley, on the other hand, suggested in late 2025 that the most aggressive portfolios should hold at most 4% in the asset. That argues for an allocation of less than 5% for most investors -- and remember, if the coin's inherent volatility is going to make you lose sleep, aim for the shallower end of that pool with your allocation. title: JPMorgan Has Returned 159% in Three Years. After Its First Miss Since 2023, Take Profits or Buy More? - TIKR.com
content: Aflo Images from アフロ（Aflo) and Ca-ssis from Getty Images via Canva JPMorgan Chase (JPM) missed on earnings. That almost never happens. Third-quarter EPS of $5.57 fell short of the roughly $5.90 consensus, the bank’s first quarterly miss in nearly three years. Yet the stock has held up, closing Friday at $337, down 1.9% on the day and about 8% below its $367 high. Investors are looking past the miss to two other numbers: a higher interest income outlook and a buyback that nearly vanished. This week added a new wrinkle. Bloomberg reported that Anthropic picked JPMorgan to lead the U.S. retail portion of its IPO, and the bank’s 55ip unit is bringing tax-aware portfolio analysis into Claude for financial advisers. Revenue held up. Managed revenue rose 8% to $50.9 billion, just shy of the $51.26 billion estimate. Expenses were the bigger issue: A $658 million securities loss also cost 18 cents a share. Excluding it, EPS was $5.75, still below the Street. Managed net interest income rose 13% to $27.1 billion on deposit growth, card balances and Markets NII. Net buybacks fell to $664 million in the quarter, down from $6.2 billion. That was a choice. Jamie Dimon said franchise investment and client support come first, and he expressed confidence the bank can deploy that capital at attractive returns over time. The standardized CET1 ratio slipped to 13.9% from 14.8% a year earlier as average loans grew 10% to $1.6 trillion. Shareholders still got a raise. The quarterly dividend rose to $1.65 from $1.50. Dimon also listed what worries him: large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising rates and geopolitics. Those warnings help explain why he wants a cushion. Here’s what that pullback looks like against recent quarters: Mandates like Anthropic’s IPO are the kind of business that spending is meant to win. Wealth management is another target, with $263 billion of net client inflows in the quarter. TIKR tracks 26 analysts on JPMorgan Chase. How many say “Buy”? For the fourth quarter, it expects about $28 billion of total NII. Its central case for 2027 calls for roughly $107 billion of NII excluding Markets. Expenses keep climbing as well, with full-year adjusted expense now guided to about $108.6 billion. JPMorgan trades at 13.4x forward earnings. In April it fetched 14.3x, against 11.9x for Bank of America and 11.4x for Wells Fargo, and a 20% ROTCE still supports that gap. My take: The miss came from spending Dimon chose to make, and I’m comfortable with that trade while NII guidance keeps rising. JPMorgan JPM has raised its net interest income (NII) outlook for 2026, supported by steady loan growth, higher deposit balances and resilient customer activity. The banking giant also provided an encouraging preliminary NII outlook for 2027, suggesting that spread income momentum could continue into next year.In the third quarter of 2026, JPMorgan's NII increased 13% year over year to $27.1 billion. Its diversified business model, strong capital position and robust profitability further support its growth prospects. However, rising operating expenses, credit-related risks and a premium valuation remain concerns. Against this backdrop, should investors consider buying JPM shares? JPMorgan's NII prospects have strengthened considerably, reflecting favorable business trends and an improving interest-rate outlook. Following its third-quarter results, management raised its full-year 2026 total NII projection to approximately $106.2 billion from the previously expected $105.5 billion.Similarly, NII excluding Markets is now anticipated to reach approximately $97.2 billion, up from the earlier projection of $96.5 billion. For the fourth quarter, management expects total NII of roughly $28 billion and NII excluding Markets of $25.5 billion.JPMorgan provided a preliminary central-case outlook for 2027 NII excluding Markets of approximately $107 billion. This suggests growth of roughly 10% from the implied 2026 level, signaling management's confidence in continued business expansion.The upbeat outlook is supported by sustained growth in lending and deposits, along with expectations of a favorable interest-rate environment. Higher loan balances and improved yields on interest-earning assets are expected to support interest income, while JPMorgan's extensive deposit franchise provides a competitive funding advantage. Nonetheless, management emphasized that its 2027 projections remain preliminary and depend on several economic and market assumptions. JPMorgan's robust balance sheet expansion reinforces its optimistic NII outlook. In the third quarter of 2026, average loans increased 10% year over year to $1.6 trillion, while average deposits grew 8% to $2.7 trillion.NII excluding Markets advanced 6% year over year to $24.7 billion, driven by higher deposit balances, increased credit card balances and growth in wholesale lending. These factors more than offset the adverse impact of lower interest rates.Continued lending demand across consumer and commercial businesses, coupled with deposit growth, is expected to support interest-earning asset expansion. Moreover, JPMorgan's diversified deposit base and established customer relationships provide a relatively stable funding source, strengthening its ability to sustain spread income.The improving NII outlook is not limited to JPMorgan. Bank of America BAC expects full-year 2026 NII on a fully taxable-equivalent (FTE) basis to grow approximately 8% year over year, with growth of 8% or more anticipated for 2027. Likewise, Citigroup C now expects NII excluding Markets to grow in the mid-to-high 6% range in 2026, an improvement from its previous forecast of growth at the high end of the 5-6% range.These encouraging projections indicate broader NII growth opportunities across major U.S. banks, supported by loan and deposit expansion and asset repricing. However, changes in interest rates, deposit pricing and economic conditions could influence the extent of future gains. Diversified Operations Drive Strong Results: JPMorgan's investment appeal extends beyond its improving NII prospects. Its commercial and investment banking, markets, payments, credit card and asset management businesses provide multiple sources of earnings.The company generated net income of approximately $53 billion in the first nine months of 2026, supported by broad-based strength across its businesses. Results also reflected third-quarter investment securities losses and second-quarter gains related to Visa shares and certain equity investments.The Commercial & Investment Bank delivered particularly strong results. Revenues for the first nine months climbed 20% year over year to $71 billion, while investment banking fees rose 33%. Markets revenues increased 23%, aided by a 49% surge in equities revenues. Management indicated that the investment banking pipeline remained robust and expected activity levels to stay healthy, subject to market conditions.Similarly, Asset & Wealth Management performed well, with revenues rising 15% and assets under management reaching $5.21 trillion as of Sept. 30, 2026. Strong net inflows and higher market levels supported management fees, providing another source of income less directly tied to lending spreads.Capital Strength Supports Shareholder Returns: JPMorgan ended the third quarter with a standardized common equity Tier 1 ratio of 13.9%, underscoring its solid capital position and ability to withstand potential economic or credit-related stress.The company authorized a new $50 billion share repurchase program, effective July 1, 2026, and increased its quarterly dividend by 10% to $1.65 per share. JPMorgan's capital strength enables it to reward shareholders while continuing to invest in technology, branches, bankers and other growth initiatives.Similarly, Bank of America increased its quarterly dividend by 14% to 32 cents per share, while Citigroup raised its payout by 11.7% to 67 cents per share.Rising Expenses and Credit Risks Remain Concerns: Despite improving NII prospects and diversified revenue streams, JPMorgan faces challenges from rising operating expenses and credit-related uncertainties.In the first nine months of 2026, non-interest expenses increased 14% year over year to $81.5 billion, driven by higher compensation costs, technology investments and business expansion. Management also raised its full-year 2026 adjusted expense forecast to approximately $108.6 billion from $107.5 billion, primarily reflecting higher expenses associated with stronger business volumes and revenues.Although continued investments in technology, branches and personnel will likely support long-term growth, elevated spending could affect operating leverage and limit the benefits of higher NII in the near term.Credit-related risks also remain a concern. In the first nine months, provision for credit losses rose 20% to $53 billion. Potential economic weakness, deterioration in borrowers' repayment capacity and changes in interest rates could further pressure asset quality and profitability. JPMorgan shares have gained 6.6% so far this year, outperforming the industry's 1.3% growth. During the same period, Bank of America shares have declined 7.1%, while Citigroup has gained 7.7%. However, JPMorgan's valuation appears relatively expensive. The stock currently trades at a trailing 12-month price-to-tangible book (P/TB) multiple of 3.22X, higher than the industry's 3.03X. In comparison, Citigroup and Bank of America trade at considerably lower multiples of 1.27X and 1.82X, respectively. The premium valuation reflects JPMorgan's strong profitability, diversified operations and leading market position. Nevertheless, it could limit near-term upside, particularly if earnings growth moderates or expenses remain elevated.The Zacks Consensus Estimate for JPMorgan's 2026 earnings indicates 22.8% year-over-year growth, while 2027 earnings are projected to rise 3.6%. Over the past week, earnings estimates for 2026 and 2027 have remained unchanged at $24.97 and $25.87 per share, respectively. Although earnings growth expectations remain positive, the relatively modest projected increase for 2027 and lack of recent upward estimate revisions suggest that much of the favorable operating outlook may already be reflected in JPMorgan's valuation. JPMorgan's improved NII outlook for 2026 and encouraging preliminary projections for 2027 strengthen its earnings visibility. Robust lending and deposit growth, diversified revenue streams and a solid capital position should support profitability and shareholder returns over the long term.However, elevated operating expenses, credit-related uncertainties and the stock's premium valuation could limit near-term upside. Moreover, relatively modest earnings growth expectations for 2027 and unchanged consensus estimates suggest limited catalysts for substantial near-term appreciation.Hence, despite JPMorgan's strong fundamentals and improving NII prospects, its current valuation does not appear to offer a particularly compelling entry point. Existing investors may consider retaining their positions, while prospective investors could wait for a more attractive valuation before buying JPM shares.At present, JPMorgan carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). content: ① Morgan Asset Management is optimistic about the long-term demand for AI, focusing on returns across the industry chain and application opportunities; ② U.S. equity earnings are expected to broaden by 2027, with bonds, energy, and infrastructure attracting attention; ③ Active ETFs are targeting income and downside protection, while alternative investments emphasize liquidity. Cailian Press, October 30 (Reporter Wu Yuqi): "We aim to engage in AI‑driven investing, while also ensuring that not everything is reliant on AI," said Paul Quinsee, Global Head of Equities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, during the 2026 J.P. Morgan Asset Management Asia-Pacific Media Summit held in Singapore, as he outlined the firm's investment strategy for 2027. Paul Quinsee, Global Head of Equities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management AI remains one of the most discussed investment themes at this summit. Several investment professionals at J.P. Morgan Asset Management maintain a positive outlook on AI's long-term demand, but when it comes to whether capital expenditures will translate into corporate profitability, when investment returns will trickle down to end‑users, and what opportunities lie beyond tech stocks, heads of different business units offer varied perspectives. For investors already heavily allocated to U.S. technology stocks, J.P. Morgan Asset Management recommends seeking additional sources of return across investment styles, regions, and asset classes. Beyond equities, bond coupons, energy infrastructure, healthcare, and private‑market investments are all drawing attention. On the product side, actively managed ETFs are being deployed to address specific investment needs such as cash‑flow generation and downside protection, while, with private markets becoming more accessible to high‑net‑worth clients, the liquidity of underlying assets has also emerged as a key area of discussion. AI demand remains robust, and investment opportunities are spreading throughout the industry chain. Whether AI capital expenditures can be sustained was the central focus of this summit. Geng Ngarmboonanant, Deputy Head of Multi‑Asset Solutions Research and Head of Macro and Policy Research at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, believes that AI‑related capital spending and resilient U.S. consumer demand continue to underpin economic growth. He forecasts that U.S. GDP growth will decelerate to around 2% over the next 12 months. Fiscal tax rebates, a stabilizing labor market, and the wealth effect from equity markets are expected to remain supportive of consumption. Regarding inflation, Geng Ngarmboonanant believes that current pressures stem primarily from supply-side shocks such as tariffs and energy costs. If these shocks gradually subside, inflation is expected to ease; however, it remains important to monitor whether rising energy prices trigger second-round effects. From a corporate perspective, Jason Yum, an equity research analyst and portfolio manager in the United States, argues that a single, uniform return on investment cannot be used to assess the entire AI industry value chain. Jason Yum, U.S. equity research analyst and portfolio manager He pointed out that the costs associated with data center construction—such as equipment, networking, and power—are relatively easy to estimate; the real source of significant variation lies in the revenue generated per unit of computing power. While some cloud‑infrastructure businesses deliver decent returns on investment, their operations remain far from straightforward; by contrast, certain cutting‑edge model developers boast unit‑level economic performance that is considerably more attractive. Regarding the trend of tech giants ramping up debt‑financed investments in AI, Jason Yum argues that such decisions should be evaluated in light of a company's operating cash flow and overall leverage levels. One should not conclude that these investments lack returns simply because capital expenditures are rising and free cash flow has turned negative. Feedback from Asian supply chains indicates that AI-related demand remains robust. Oliver Cox, Portfolio Manager for Emerging Markets and Asia-Pacific Equities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said that during recent visits to Asian companies, his team found that supply has yet to fully catch up with demand, with actual demand continuing to exceed earlier expectations. He remains optimistic that the AI‑related capital‑expenditure cycle will persist for an extended period, and that opportunities extend beyond the chip sector: semiconductor materials, substrates, packaging and testing, as well as networking equipment, all harbor companies worthy of attention. Oliver Cox, Portfolio Manager for Emerging Markets and Asia-Pacific Equities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management However, Oliver Cox also cautions that a long-term bullish outlook on AI does not preclude short-term volatility in related stocks, and it is unwise to assume that companies with strong past performance will continue to lead. Jason Yum is adopting a more optimistic stance toward AI applications. He believes that the revenue generated by AI need not merely replace traditional software markets; many workflows previously performed manually could also open up new market opportunities for software companies. Familiar user interfaces, robust security measures, and well‑established management frameworks will help enterprise customers further embrace AI. Oliver Cox also focuses on changes at the application level. He notes that, at present, the AI industry's primary sources of revenue and growth remain concentrated in semiconductors and data centers; as technology advances, higher returns are expected to gradually shift toward the application layer. In the Asian market, there are already examples of AI enhancing operational efficiency in areas such as human resources software, gaming, and IT services. Xu Changtai, Chief Market Strategist for Asia-Pacific at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, believes that corporate adoption of AI remains in its early stages. Following the rollout of new tools by the technology function, finance leaders will conduct a thorough review of costs and returns, while security and governance teams will also weigh in on decision‑making. As a result, companies may adopt a more cautious approach at certain phases, which could temper the pace of short‑term adoption. U.S. equity opportunities are expanding to more companies, and there is also room for deployment in the bond and private‑equity markets. Regarding the stock market in 2027, Paul Quinsee remains relatively optimistic, with his outlook largely grounded in corporate earnings. He observed that earnings growth is spreading across more markets and companies, and U.S. equity markets are no longer driven solely by a handful of large tech firms; an increasing number of companies, including small-cap stocks, are now taking part. For investors who have already increased their U.S. asset allocations—particularly those holding substantial positions in large-cap technology stocks—Paul Quinsee recommends enhancing diversification across both style and region, seeking opportunities in value‑oriented strategies, as well as in Europe, Japan, and emerging markets. Paul Quinsee also closely monitors the sustainability of AI‑related capital expenditures. Large‑scale investments require robust funding, and their implementation may be constrained by physical limitations and policy considerations. The technology sector's competitive landscape evolves rapidly; today's market leaders may not be able to sustain their advantage over the long term, underscoring the need for ongoing fundamental analysis. In the fixed-income market, Bob Michele, Chief Investment Officer and Head of Global Fixed Income, Currencies, and Commodities at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, places great value on the coupon income that bonds can currently deliver. He believes that bond investments can generate coupon income and, should yields decline in the future, may also deliver capital gains from price appreciation. Beyond the United States, markets such as Japan and Australia offer attractive opportunities as well. Duration management, positioning along the yield curve, and credit selection are all areas where active management can add value. Regarding AI‑related financing, Bob Michele stressed the need to differentiate between borrowers' risk profiles. Companies with established operations and robust operating cash flows do not face the same credit risks as entities that rely heavily on the delivery of future projects and the realization of commercial revenues. He also identified persistent inflationary pressures and sharp interest‑rate hikes as tail risks—though relatively low in probability, they warrant close attention. In the private markets, Jed Laskowitz, Global Head of Private Markets and Customized Solutions at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, is optimistic about the long-term investment demand in energy and infrastructure. He believes that this demand stems not only from the construction of AI‑powered data centers, but also from broader trends such as electrification, the energy transition, and the growing emphasis on energy security across nations. Healthcare and life sciences are likewise key areas of focus. AI is driving advances in drug discovery, and major pharmaceutical companies are bolstering their product pipelines through acquisitions of smaller firms, creating opportunities for private‑equity investment in this space. Charles Wu, Head of the Alternative Investment Strategy Team for Asia-Pacific at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, is particularly bullish on core infrastructure. He notes that these assets deliver essential public services, and for some projects, revenue over the next 10 to 15 years can be highly predictable thanks to regulated tariffs or long-term contracts. Regulated utilities in the United States also remain a key area of focus, as tightening electricity supply is creating attractive investment opportunities. In the private equity space, James Burdis, Head of Global Strategic Relationships and Alternative Investments for Private Wealth at J.P. Morgan Asset Management's Asia-Pacific region, places greater emphasis on investing in small and medium-sized enterprises. He believes that fund managers can create value by enhancing operational efficiency, and that exit strategies need not rely solely on IPOs; they can also exit by selling companies to other private equity firms. Active ETFs place greater emphasis on investment objectives, while alternative investments require managing liquidity expectations. In addition to asset allocation strategies, how to tailor products to meet diverse investment needs was also a key topic at this summit. According to data cited by Philippe El-Asmar, Head of ETFs, Digitalization, and Direct Sales for Asia-Pacific at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, actively managed ETFs currently account for roughly 11.4% of the global ETF market size, yet they already represent nearly 30% of net inflows into ETFs. In his view, the ETF industry is evolving from passive index tracking and active investment management to a stage where products are designed around specific investment outcomes. He refers to this shift as "ETF 3.0." Investors no longer simply choose which index to track; they can first define their investment objectives—such as generating cash flow or managing downside risk—and then select strategies that align with those goals. Hamilton Reiner, Chief Investment Officer of Morgan Asset Management's U.S. Core Equity Team and Head of U.S. Equity Derivatives Strategy, explains that the fundamental trade-off in options‑based income strategies is to forgo some of the potential upside in exchange for current income. During market rallies, this type of strategy typically captures only a portion of the gains; when markets decline, stock selection and option premiums help cushion losses; and in sideways markets, dividends and option premiums serve as key sources of income. Hamilton Reiner emphasized that strategy design must balance cash flow with participation in market upside, and should not prioritize income distributions at the expense of eroding the fund's net asset value. Investors need to thoroughly understand a product's return and risk profile across different market environments. Regarding the Asian actively managed ETF market, Philippe El-Asmar noted that different regions still have varying requirements in areas such as derivatives usage, portfolio transparency, and tracking error relative to benchmarks, and that ongoing investor education will be essential for the sector's continued development. The private‑placement market is opening further to high‑net‑worth clients, and it likewise requires addressing the alignment between product structures and the characteristics of underlying assets. Jed Laskowitz, Global Head of Private Markets and Customized Solutions at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, cautions that structuring private‑market assets within products that offer certain redemption provisions does not alter the liquidity of the underlying assets themselves. Charles Wu likewise stresses that, for wealth clients new to alternative investments, managing liquidity expectations is especially critical. Dan Watkins, CEO of Morgan Asset Management for the Asia-Pacific region, also noted in the opening discussion that expanding investment channels in the private markets requires first taking into account clients' liquidity needs, risk profiles, and investment objectives. Regarding the asset management industry's own development, Dan Watkins also discussed the changes brought about by AI. He believes that AI models and tools will gradually become standard across the sector, with differentiation among asset managers increasingly hinging on how they leverage data, derive investment insights, and implement effective AI governance. Dan Watkins also emphasized that global investment capabilities must remain aligned with local execution. As the industry continues to evolve, maintaining curiosity, a willingness to keep asking probing questions, and the ability—and psychological resilience—to adapt to change are all critical for both employees and leaders at asset management firms. Any investor could write up a long list of market risks—whether it’s questions over spending on artificial intelligence, financing the build-out and profitability timelines, or strain in European government bond markets. Add on uncertainty around the U.S. midterm elections and renewed fears of military escalation in Iran, which could happen shortly after. And yet, the S&P 500 remains within 1% of its all-time high—again. Resilience doesn’t come without volatility, especially when the calendar is filled with risk events: high profile catalysts that could determine the trajectory of conflict in the Middle East, the signals around the AI build-out or even some of the plumbing in international markets. But with the risks well known, investors typically hedge in anticipation. That often means these market moments act as clearing events—a point where uncertainty or pressure in financial markets gets resolved, allowing investors to reposition, typically setting the stage for gains. The October Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting and subsequent rate hold is an example of a market event with the potential for market volatility that ultimately yielded little price movement. And this time, historical performance is on the side of investors seeking a jolly mood into the holiday season. Over the last 29 years, the S&P 500 has averaged 2.3% in November, the strongest of any calendar month. Those returns are even larger in midterm election cycles, with November yielding an average 2.75% returns when the White House isn’t on the ballot. In the six months that follow, the S&P 500 has averaged gains of about 13%. The 2026 midterm election cycle has two key long-term market implications—both of which may already be priced in by investors. The first is the debate around AI, which has moved beyond whether the technology is useful. Investors increasingly want to know how much infrastructure will be built, who will finance it and when the spending will generate sufficient returns to make the investment worth it. A key element of that trade is the power supply, which has put utilities—a traditionally defensive and stable sector—at the heart of the AI build-out. Investors have long worried about a federal freeze on the data center build-out, based on how Congress is made up after the midterm election. But over the summer, many of the fears of what would happen on a national level trickled down to the state level, where most of the public backlash was felt. New York and Texas—two states on opposite sides of the political spectrum—both announced a data center moratorium, that served as an overhang on the utilities sector. The second implication is in fiscal spend, as the United States enters the midterm elections with little fiscal room to maneuver. These spending priorities are significant in light of a potentially mixed Congress. The political pendulum tends to swing away from the party in power, with majority control changing hands in at least one chamber of Congress. That has been the result in three of the past four midterm elections. Whereas ordinarily that means little to no policy change, in some cases, gridlock doesn’t reduce spending but amplifies it instead. In the face of a true impasse, lawmakers can be encouraged to fund priorities from both parties – yielding more spending, not less. In a world where global bond markets are sensitive to growing government deficits, this dynamic can have long-term consequences on the term premium commanded by investors to hold U.S. government debt. And that can have ripple effects into other financial markets, especially stocks. Even in the face of ongoing risks, the stock market is showing early signs of breadth. Realized correlations between stocks remain low, which means stock performance is differentiated to some degree and individual stocks aren’t all moving in the same direction at the same time. While the Nasdaq 100 fell as much as 8% in October from peak to trough and later recouped its losses, the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index rose approximately 4% over the same month. The number of S&P 500 stocks hitting new 20-day highs has exceeded 50% for the first time since the second quarter of 2025. That kind of broad-based price action has historically preceded further gains in equities on both a three-month and six-month basis. JPMorgan Chase is the largest bank in the United States by assets, offering consumer banking, commercial lending, capital markets services, payments, and asset and wealth management. Its operations span retail branches, credit cards, corporate finance, trading, and advisory work for businesses and institutions worldwide. As a leading  financial stock, JPMorgan is widely viewed as a barometer for consumer spending, corporate borrowing, capital markets activity, and credit quality across the American economy. JPMorgan's latest quarter delivered diluted  earnings per share ahead of the year-earlier level, reflecting strength across several of its businesses. Managed revenue rose meaningfully, supported by both lending and fee-based activities. The results reinforced JPMorgan's reputation for consistent execution, as the bank continues to benefit from its scale, diversified business mix, and strong position across consumer and corporate banking. Net interest income, the difference between what the bank earns on loans and securities and what it pays on deposits, is JPMorgan's largest single revenue line. The latest figure represented a notable step up from a year earlier, driven by several forces, including loan growth and balance sheet positioning. Strong net interest income gives JPMorgan a powerful foundation, funding everything from technology spending to dividends and capital returns. Noninterest revenue, which includes trading, advisory fees, card fees, and asset management fees, grew at a more modest pace than net interest income. That pattern shows lending remains the primary growth driver, while fee businesses contributed steady but smaller increases.
